In [[mathematics]], the '''orbit capacity''' of a subset of a [[topological dynamical system]] may be thought of heuristically as a “topological dynamical [[probability measure]]” of the subset. More precisely, its value for a set is a tight upper bound for the normalized number of visits of orbits in this set.

== Definition ==

A topological dynamical system consists of a [[compact space|compact]] [[Hausdorff space|Hausdorff]] [[topological space]] ''X'' and a [[homeomorphism]] <math>T:X\rightarrow X</math>. Let <math>E\subset X</math> be a set. [[Elon Lindenstrauss|Lindenstrauss]] introduced the definition of orbit capacity:<ref>{{Cite journal|title = Mean dimension, small entropy factors and an embedding theorem|journal = Publications Mathématiques de l'Institut des Hautes Études Scientifiques|date = 1999-12-01|issn = 0073-8301|page = 232|volume = 89|issue = 1|doi = 10.1007/BF02698858|first = Elon|last = Lindenstrauss|url = http://www.numdam.org/item/PMIHES_1999__89__227_0/}}</ref>

:<math>\operatorname{ocap}(E)=\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\sup_{x\in X} \frac 1 n \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} \chi_E (T^k x)</math>

Here, <math>\chi_E(x)</math> is the [[membership function]] for the set <math>E</math>. That is <math>\chi_E(x)=1</math> if <math>x\in E</math> and is zero otherwise. 

== Properties ==
One has <math>0\le\operatorname{ocap}(E)\le 1</math>. By convention, topological dynamical systems do not come equipped with a [[measure (mathematics)|measure]]; the orbit capacity can be thought of as defining one, in a "natural" way. It is not a true measure, it is only a sub-additive:

* Orbit capacity is [[Subadditivity|sub-additive]]:

:: <math>\operatorname{ocap}(A\cup B)\leq \operatorname{ocap}(A)+\operatorname{ocap}(B)</math>

* For a closed set ''C'',

:: <math>\operatorname{ocap}(C)=\sup_{\mu\in \operatorname{M}_T(X)}\mu(C)</math>

: Where M<sub>''T''</sub>(''X'') is the collection of ''T''-[[invariant measure|invariant probability measure]]s on&nbsp;''X''.
== Small sets ==
When <math>\operatorname{ocap}(A)=0</math>, <math>A</math> is called '''small'''. These sets occur in the definition of the [[small boundary property]].
